item.title: Are You a Spiritual Pig-Pen?
item.description:
Stress

Are You a Spiritual Pig-Pen?

What you’re carrying may be making you sick.

Posted August 25, 2026

Today I was thinking about the concept of 'spiritual hygiene.' How many of you remember Pig-Pen from Charlie Brown? When we were growing up, and I know I'm dating myself, Pig-Pen was this character in the Peanuts gang that always had a cloud of smoke around him. Wherever he went, there was a cloud of dirt. He was part of the Peanuts gang, he was in the crew, but he was also looked at very disdainfully. As kids, we thought that was funny. As adults, It’s not so funny.

Now I’m thinking about Pig-Pen as a metaphor for somebody that's in need of spiritual hygiene. I'm sure younger generations have something that they call that, right? It's usually the person who trauma dumps on everyone, like in the group chat in the middle of the night. Usually that person who has weird energy, and when they walk in the room, people are thinking, “Oh, here they go again!” Or the person that you know is going to say something negative about the situation instead of thinking positively. It's okay to talk about what's going on, but that person constantly has to be negative. There's no way that they can look at things in a positive light. Maybe young people just call that person “draining.”

Are you a spiritual Pig-Pen? Not in your hygiene but in your energy, your spirit, in the invisible weight you carry into every room, every relationship. Every attempt at rest, the unresolved grief never spoken aloud, the inherited anger, the shame woven into the family. I remember when movies like Rosewood came out, and people would say, "Oh, I don't want to watch that, because it's so negative. Even though it’s about our history." As you know, African people living in America need to address what happened; some people just want to forget it, it's in the past and they don't want to address it. They say, “I don't want to see any more of those “slave movies”. Well, the history has not been fully processed, and we may still be carrying it in our current time period. Believe it or not, we are still dealing with the emotional, physical, economic, and political ramifications of that period of enslavement. This spiritual dirt, it's things that we have not processed; sometimes also things that we have not processed in our family, in our community, in the world. We move through the world dragging the spiritual dirt behind us. Most of us have no idea it's there, but our bodies do. And the science now confirms what our ancestors always knew. You carry things spiritually and physically, and it can make you sick, and it could even make your children sick. If we do not address it, it can make their children sick.

Spiritual dirt has a clinical name. Scientists call it allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear on the body produced by chronic stress that never gets processed or released. Think of it as a physical price your body pays for everything you refuse to put down or let go. Every unprocessed loss, every relationship that kept your nervous system on high alert. Every grief you swallow adds weight to the load.  

Research found that unresolved grief alone can dysregulate the body's stress response systems, producing elevated cortisol and inflammatory markers that persist for months or even years, increasing risk for autoimmune disorders, cardiovascular disease, and depression. Studies show that up to 80% of patients with autoimmune disorders experience significant emotional stress before their diagnosis. This is not a metaphor. This is real. This is measurable in blood and tissue as an accelerating biological agent. The cloud is not invisible in the body. The body sees it clearly and pays the price.

For young people, the stakes are especially high. Research shows that chronic stress during adolescence, when the brain and nervous system are still developing, produces lasting physiological changes. The youth mental health crisis we are living through is not simply a social media problem or a pandemic hangover. It is a significant problem, a spiritual dirt problem, a generation of young people carrying inherited pain with no tools to process.

Long before Western medicine had the language of allostatic load, previous generations had the wisdom to address what we are now measuring in labs. When I study the African and African diaspora, I see spiritual cleansing is not superstition. It was preventative healthcare. Ritual baths with herbs, practiced in the Afro-Caribbean, Brazil and West African traditions, were prescribed for physical, spiritual, and emotional ailments because African traditions didn’t make the mistake of treating them as separate. Healing circles bring community together around those who are suffering, recognizing that you cannot heal alone. Smudging and burning of sacred herbs were used, not just sage, to clear the energy of our spaces. Not as ceremony, just for the sake of ceremony, but a deliberate intervention with the body and spirit.

These practices were not primitive. They were sophisticated ancestral technologies operating on the same principle that modern science is now confirming: how the mind, body, and spirit are not separate systems. They are one system, and you cannot treat one while ignoring the others. The ancestral healers who practice these rituals understood that you had to address what you were carrying before you could heal what it had damaged. You had to give voice to it first.

The dirt you don't see is still dirty. That's what makes spiritual Pig-Pen so common and dangerous.  Most people don't know they are even spiritual Pig-Pen. We have normalized the dust and the dirt. We call it a personality. Oh, I'm just an anxious person. I've always had a short fuse. I'm entitled to do what I want even if it hurts other people. I don't really process things. I just push through. We mistake the cloud for character, and our children inherit both the cloud and the mistaken belief that it belongs to them.  

The grief you didn't grieve doesn't disappear. It goes somewhere. It becomes inflammation, insomnia, and autoimmune conditions that appear out of nowhere. The depression you can't explain because your life looks fine from the outside. It becomes the 2 a.m. group chat message your teenager sends because they have nowhere else to put what they're feeling. It becomes a pattern in your family that everyone notices, and no one is able to voice. To be sure, spiritual cleansing is not a substitute for clinical care. If you or your child are living with depression, anxiety, trauma, or chronic illness, ancestral healing practices are not a replacement for therapy or medicine. They are a powerful, evidence informed addition to it. The World Health Organization has recognized traditional and indigenous healing systems as legitimate components of comprehensive healthcare. In fact, over 80% of the world's population uses traditional and natural medicine.  

The science of psychoneuroimmunology is confirming and addressing the emotional and spiritual dimensions of health. It produces measurable physiological results. The ritual bath and therapy session are not in competition. They are colleagues. And it's time to clean up. Pig-Pen was beloved; he was cheerful, genuine, goodhearted, but nobody wanted to stand too close. The longer he went without addressing his cloud, the more it became his identity. Growing up, we just thought it was his identity until the dirt and the person were indistinguishable. You are not your unresolved grief. Your child is not their anxiety. Neither of you is the cloud you've been carrying since before you were born. Since before you knew you were carrying it, but you will keep. But you will keep being mistaken for it, and so will they, until someone in the family decides to set it down, until someone makes a choice.

Our ancestors built the tools, the herbs, the water, the fire, the circle, the song, the conversation across dinner about what this family carries and what we are choosing to release. These are technologies of spiritual hygiene designed to do what no prescription alone can accomplish. Clear what the body is holding, so the healing can begin. The cloud is real; the cost is miserable. It takes time to clean it up. Not only cleaning your house, but your spirit, your energy. Not for your sake alone, but for the young people watching you carrying the dirt and for every generation that comes after.

item.title: As AI Gets Smarter, Being Human Matters More
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

As AI Gets Smarter, Being Human Matters More

In an AI-fueled world, we need to develop the skills technology can't do for us.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • AI can support emotional well-being, but it cannot replace human connection.
  • Human connection requires presence, empathy, and compassion.
  • Emotional skills improve through intentional practice.
Source: Gigi Gupta / Used with permission

In the world of AI, it is becoming increasingly essential that we begin to pay more attention to the qualities that make us human: the compassion we bring to the workplace, the emotional intelligence we have as leaders to help influence change within the people around us, and our lived experiences that influence how we interact with others and solve problems. As AI becomes increasingly sophisticated, it becomes more important that we learn to better leverage these strengths.

To find out more, I interviewed Gigi Gupta, a former start-up CEO, executive coach, and meditation teacher who now works in AI. Her experience offers a unique perspective on what technology can replicate and what makes us human.

Where Can AI Help With Emotions?

When life challenges arise, we have seen a growing trend that many people may seek support from tools like chatbots. In fact, a recent study found that people may be willing to disclose more intimate information to chatbots, in part because they are accessible, convenient, anonymous, and perceived as nonjudgmental. AI can support emotional well-being through pattern recognition, identifying emotional themes, and recognizing signs that may suggest someone could benefit from additional support.

Where AI Reaches Its Limits

Although AI can be supportive, we know that it should not replace professional judgement, and should only be used as a tool, not as a substitute for evaluation or treatment. "You cannot outsource your presence," Gupta says. "You can outsource the analysis, the drafting, the modeling. You cannot outsource being the steady person in a room full of anxious people." The human presence is unique as it provides empathy, compassion, human judgment, and behavior cues that are vital for genuine connection. For instance, a chatbot can identify themes in prompts that demonstrate frustration and dissatisfaction at work. However, even when additional context is provided, it is limited to what is input and does not have data regarding nonverbal cues, interpersonal dynamics, or other factors that the person may not even recognize. If the information provided is incomplete or reflects a particular perspective, AI may inadvertently reinforce that perspective, providing only a partial picture of the situation.

The Human Skill We Still Have to Practice

Therefore, as AI continues to grow in popularity and usage, it is important for us to intentionally cultivate the human skills we hold. Research suggests that emotional competencies are not simply fixed traits; they can be developed through intentional practice. When was the last time you were intentional when it came to improving your listening skills, communication, and emotional regulation? AI may be able to provide us with ideas on how to strengthen these skills, but it is up to us to practice engaging in these behaviors. Gupta describes building that skill as unglamorous: meditation, reflection, the pause between a thought and a response. Taking a moment before responding can make a difference, especially when things get stressful. That brief pause gives us time to listen, consider what the other person is saying, manage our emotions, and respond thoughtfully.

Why Human Connection May Become More Valuable

In this day and age, it is not challenging to obtain more information. However, during times of stress, what we often need as humans is connection, someone willing to listen, and to feel understood. Gupta sees this in her own work. “Caring too much about your people has never been what burns leaders out,” she says. “They burn out when they never learn their own steadiness was part of the job.” Being there for others starts with managing yourself. As technology handles more of the work, our ability to show up for each other becomes even more important. In the workplace, this may look like checking in on a colleague you have noticed has been withdrawn, or asking someone how they are really feeling rather than simply giving a standard, “Good morning, how are you?” These small but powerful actions can go a long way in helping people feel seen, heard, and valued.

Action Steps

Here are some practical ways to build the emotional skills that technology cannot replace:

  1. Practice active listening: I am sure you can think of a time when you jumped to conclusions during a conversation, or had an assumption that you later recognized was inaccurate. Therefore, next time try to focus on understanding before thinking about how you will respond. Ask yourself, “What am I missing, and what else do I need to understand before I respond?”

  2. Ask better questions: When at work, move beyond “How are you?” and ask questions that invite honest conversation with colleagues. For instance, asking deep questions like “What did you enjoy most about your weekend?” or asking “What is one thing you are looking forward to?” can help move conversations beyond small talk and create opportunities for people to share what matters to them.

  3. Pay attention to behavior changes: Being mindful of behavioral changes is essential to further strengthen our emotional intelligence and leverage our superpowers as humans. For instance, begin to notice when someone's tone, engagement, or behavior seems different from usual. A colleague who is normally talkative may become unusually quiet, or someone who is typically engaged may seem distracted or withdrawn. This can open up an opportunity to offer support and reach out to let the person know that you noticed a change and are available to listen if they would like to talk. Sometimes, simply knowing that someone noticed and cares can make a meaningful difference.

Bottom Line

As AI continues to advance, we must use our strengths in a more intentional way within our workplaces and personal relationships. Whether it be spending more time with our loved ones or paying more attention to the well-being of our colleagues, we can all better leverage the parts of us that make us human. This will boost our connection with others, grow our relationships, and provide the support that others need, something that only we can do.
